title: Strength gone, in chains
hookLine: strength is gone, I'm in chains, nothing works; Nanak says, only You are my refuge (Salok M9 53, ang 1429)

cards: The calls have been made, the forms filled out, the advice taken, and the problem is still sitting there. A diagnosis. A job search in its ninth month.
A child who won't talk to you. Everything known has been tried, and at some point a person hears themselves say, out loud or not: I've got nothing left. It's a strange, bare place.
Pride doesn't work there; cleverness doesn't either. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a salok from exactly that place, and Sikh tradition hears it as the words of a man in a cell.

teach.h: BAL CHHUTKIO: STRENGTH HAS SLIPPED AWAY.

teach.b: In paraphrase: my strength is exhausted, I am bound in chains, and nothing I try works.

teach.h: OT: THE SHELTER YOU LEAN ON.
teach.b: Nanak says, now You are my shelter, Lord: help me, as You helped the elephant. Three phrases do the work. Bal chhutkio: strength has slipped away.
Bandhan pare: the bonds have fallen on me. Kachhoo na hot upaai: no remedy, no plan, nothing works. It's an honest inventory, with nothing dressed up.
Then the turn: ab ot. Now, the shelter. Ot means a refuge, a support, the wall you put your back against.
And the salok adds an old picture, gaj, the elephant. Indian tradition tells of an elephant king seized by a crocodile in a lake. He pulled for a long time with all his great strength and lost.
Only when he gave up pulling and called on God was he freed. Gurbani recalls this story as a sign of grace for the helpless. Why does this salok weigh so much for Sikhs?
Tradition places it in the Guru's last months, when he was imprisoned in Delhi before his execution, and Sikhs hear it as written in real chains.
Historians don't know exactly when each salok was composed, so that link is tradition. Either way, the shape is the point. The salok doesn't pretend strength is limitless.
It admits the end of strength, and from there it asks. In Sikh thought, that asking isn't failure. It's where the ot, the shelter, finally gets leaned on.

how: Sikhs read salok fifty-three as part of the closing saloks of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and many turn to it in illness or trouble as a plain cry for the Lord's shelter.

o: a hymn praising an elephant's great strength
an honest cry at the very end of one's strength
a curse asking that enemies lose their power

p: the bonds have fallen on me
the elephant in the old story

s: the salok pretends the speaker is still strong
it lists the end of strength honestly: bound, and nothing works.
the elephant was freed when it stopped pulling and called on God
Gurbani uses the old story as a sign of grace for the helpless.
historians know the exact day this salok was written
tradition places it in the Guru's imprisonment; the exact date isn't known.

games.q: you're the elephant, seized by the crocodile, and your strength is running out. what does the story say freed you?
o: giving up the pulling and calling on God.
waiting for the crocodile to tire.
games.why: in the story, strength lost. calling on God is what freed him, and the salok asks: help me, as You helped the elephant.

practice: Bring to mind one place where you've tried everything you know, and say it as plainly as the salok does: this is what I've tried; this is what isn't working. Then let yourself lean back, the way you'd lean against a wall.
If you pray, ask God for help in your own words, or say Waheguru; if you don't, think of one person you could ask, and picture asking them.

wordCard.voice: Strength gone. Bal chhutkio, bandhan pare: strength slipped away, the bonds fell on me, and from there, the ot, the shelter.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ot, a shelter or support; salok fifty-three turns on ab ot, now the shelter.

carryVoice: Your line: only you. At the end of strength, asking isn't failure. Day six hundred four.
